# Widget Gauntlet and Interaction Message Catalog

Yantra's browser-interaction quality gate checks generic widget behavior at both
the protocol-driver seam and the real agent-tool seam. A companion message
catalog keeps model-visible interaction advice complete, distinct, and tied to
capabilities Yantra can actually execute.

This is a maintainer and integrator feature. It adds no CLI command and does not
change any stable interaction error code.

## What It Does

### Runs a 13-fixture protocol gauntlet

The fast tier runs 13 generic HTML fixtures through the production `fillField`
engine with a JSDOM-backed `WidgetPort`. Each registry entry becomes its own
named test case and declares its semantic result and exact operation counts.

| Generic pattern                              | Verified result                                                                            | Mutations | Reads |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------: | ----: |
| Input drops its initial keystroke            | Commits `DFW`                                                                              |         3 |    34 |
| Typeahead maps a code to a display label     | Commits `Dallas` as a single offered match                                                 |         2 |    17 |
| Picker mounts a duplicate trigger            | Commits `San Jose, CA, United States`                                                      |         2 |    17 |
| Read-only date trigger opens a distant month | Commits `Dec 2, 2026` through the calendar driver                                          |         6 |    32 |
| Suggestions arrive after typing settles      | Commits `Reykjavik, Iceland`                                                               |         2 |    31 |
| Two suggestions match equally                | Refuses ambiguously, then the required follow-up commits                                   |         4 |    29 |
| Trigger routes typing to a detached overlay  | Commits the airport label and reports the actual editee                                    |         3 |    22 |
| Suggestions accept only a query prefix       | Commits the selected offered value                                                         |         4 |    75 |
| Calendar appears only after an open probe    | Commits `Dec 2, 2026` through the calendar driver                                          |         6 |    40 |
| Input rewrites text into a display mask      | Commits `(555) 123-4567` as reformatted                                                    |         1 |    33 |
| One date range is split across two inputs    | Refuses the incomplete half without changing either input, then the follow-up commits both |         4 |    40 |
| Two range triggers share one calendar        | Commits both dates after opening the range once                                            |         4 |    39 |
| Listbox mounts only its in-viewport rows     | Commits `Region 6` through the listbox driver                                              |         4 |    18 |

For an engineered refusal, the totals include both the refusal and its mandatory
follow-up. A refusal is accepted only when its `(code, cause)` has a catalog
entry and the follow-up described by its hint reaches a commit. Known
unsupported behavior cannot be registered as a passing terminal result.

The port accounting policy is exhaustive at the TypeScript boundary:

- `click`, `fill`, `clear`, `type`, `press`, and `scrollContainer` are
  mutations;
- `observe`, `evaluate`, and `evaluateOn` are reads; and
- `now` is neutral.

Scrolling a container counts as a mutation because it is page work like any
keystroke: a virtualized list mounts rows in response to it, so a read-classed
scroll would let a driver reveal an unbounded number of options for free.

Every call also appears in a per-method `byAction` breakdown. Adding a
`WidgetPort` method without classifying it fails type checking, while an extra
recovery action or diagnostic read changes a fixture's pinned total and fails
its test.

### Exercises the wrapped tool in real Chrome

The real-browser tier serves four generic fixtures over loopback, launches
system Chrome, and drives the production wrapped tools through Yantra's normal
middleware and a real `AgentBrowserController`. Two fixtures are filled through
`browser_fill_element`: a search form that replaces its input while text is
entered, and a native select the page encapsulates inside a component's open
shadow tree. The other two are clicked through `browser_click` against a
control something else owns. Every descriptor pins exact controller mutation,
read, top-level tool-call, and engine-initiated clearance totals.

The re-mounting case verifies one top-level tool call, three controller
mutations, and 13 controller reads. The form replaces its input while text is
entered, forcing the engine to reacquire the element without asking the model
for another turn. The case parses the model-visible payload, checks that
`winter coat` was committed, resolves every ref in the returned observation,
and confirms that the pre-remount ref now fails with `STALE_ELEMENT_REF`. That
post-action staleness assertion runs only for a fixture that declares a
`remountSelector`, because the contract says something only about a pattern
that remounts its controls.

The shadow-tree case commits `Express` in one controller mutation and seven
reads: once the composed tree is walked, an encapsulated native select costs
exactly what a light-DOM one costs. A dedicated case fills the same control by
its accessible name, confirms on the page itself that the commit landed inside
the shadow tree, and asserts that the traversal's internal fields
(`composedScope`, `elementIndex`, `rootNodeDepth`, `selectorIndex`) never reach
the model payload. The fixture's second host holds a _closed_ root with a
structurally identical control, and the same case asserts that control's name
appears nowhere in the observation.

This tier is `@no-llm` and is not skipped by an environment gate. Chrome
discovery remains environment-dependent, as it is for Yantra's other
real-browser tests.

### Keeps fixture coverage structural and generic

Both fixture directories are compared with their registries in both
directions. An unregistered HTML file or a registry entry with no file fails
the census, and generic pattern names must be unique.

Fixtures describe structural widget shapes rather than websites. If a fixture
records a site token as provenance, that token is permitted only inside the
file's leading HTML comment and must not occur in the fixture body or anywhere
under the core or agent production-source trees. Current fixtures otherwise
record generic patterns and, where relevant, originating run IDs.

### Catalogs model-visible interaction messages

Catalog ownership follows the production package boundary:

- core owns fill failures, browser actionability failures, and fill success
  notes; and
- agent owns registered browser-tool and shared middleware messages, including
  confirmation, budget, timeout, abort, and phase failures.

Each entry is keyed by `(surface, code, cause)` and declares its message, hint,
required detail keys, and optional engine or tool capability. The internal
`cause` chooses wording but is not serialized in fill failures.

Contract tests enforce the following current invariants:

- catalog keys and rendered messages are globally distinct;
- every message renders when supplied with its declared details, while missing
  templates or details fail explicitly;
- engine capabilities resolve to public core functions and tool capabilities
  resolve against the active wrapped-tool catalog;
- interaction-layer error-code literals in the scanned agent sources have a
  core- or agent-owned catalog entry;
- the established core error-code set remains frozen; and
- a budget result that already contains the publication remedy does not receive
  the same sentence a second time.

The catalog changes ownership and verification of existing copy; it does not
rename error codes or expose the internal failure cause.

### Enforces explicit UTF-8 assertions

Fixture and artifact text used by the gauntlet is decoded with a fatal UTF-8
decoder. Invalid CP-1252/Latin-1 byte sequences throw instead of becoming
replacement characters, and every rendered catalog message is verified through
a UTF-8 encode/decode round trip.

On Windows PowerShell 5.1, inspect these files with an explicit decoder, for
example:

```powershell
Get-Content -Encoding utf8 <path>
[System.IO.File]::ReadAllText(<path>)
```

### Gates the recovery-verdict migration

The checked-in legacy fixture preserves the previous shape in which a successful
recovery rung could carry `errorCode: null` inside a later overall failure's
`details.attempted` ledger. The current gate prohibits that nullable success form
at production tool seams: attempted entries are discriminated verdicts, and only
a failed verdict contains `error_code`. Reader tests normalize the legacy fixture
without modifying it or any existing run directory.

## How to Use It

Run the focused tiers from the repository root:

```bash
pnpm --filter @yantra/core test -- widget-regressions message-catalog
pnpm --filter @yantra/agent test -- message-catalog
pnpm --filter @yantra/e2e test -- widget-gauntlet
```

Run the complete model-free gate across workspaces with:

```bash
pnpm test:no-llm
```

When adding a protocol fixture, add its HTML file and one
`PROTOCOL_GAUNTLET` descriptor. Give it a unique generic-pattern description,
an exact outcome, and pinned mutation/read totals. An engineered refusal must
also declare a cataloged failure and a follow-up that commits.

When adding a real-browser fixture, add its HTML file and one `AGENT_GAUNTLET`
descriptor with exact mutation, read, and top-level tool-call totals. When
adding model-visible interaction copy, register its surface, code, cause,
required details, and any capability rather than introducing an untracked
inline message.

## Inputs and Outputs

The gate has no runtime CLI input. Its test registries consume fixture
descriptors containing identity, generic pattern, field intent, expected
outcome, provenance, and operation budgets.

Protocol execution produces an in-memory per-fixture result with:

- fixture file, pattern, and tier;
- `commit`, `engineered-refusal`, or `failed` outcome;
- mutation, read, and top-level tool-call totals; and
- a `byAction` per-method breakdown.

The test runner is the reporting surface. The gauntlet does not create a new
durable artifact. The real-browser tier checks the wrapped tool's existing
status, error code, and JSON `modelText` payload, but it does not recreate the
orchestrator-owned `tool-calls.jsonl` projection.

Catalog rendering returns existing model-visible message and hint text. Missing
catalog entries or required detail values throw a typed dangling-message error
instead of falling back to generic advice.

## Configuration and Permissions

The protocol and catalog tiers need no credentials, model provider, network
access, or feature-specific configuration. The real-browser tier requires a
discoverable compatible system Chrome, opens only the local fixture server,
and uses temporary run/profile state that is removed during teardown.

No fixture performs a secret fill, and all three tiers are tagged `@no-llm`.

## Limitations

- The current gallery contains 17 fixtures: 13 protocol cases and four
  real-browser wrapped-tool cases (a re-mounting search form, an open
  shadow-root native select, a page-blocking consent modal, and a
  viewport-pinned band that owns a control's click point). Both halves are
  pinned as numbers, so growing the gallery is a deliberate edit.
- A control inside a _closed_ shadow root is out of scope and is never counted
  as a pass. The platform returns `null` for `host.shadowRoot` on a closed
  root, and no piercing library and no DOM tagging is used to get around that,
  so such a control is absent from the observation rather than filtered out of
  it. The closed-root half of the open-shadow fixture is asserted as absent and
  contributes no gallery entry.
- The real-browser harness validates the wrapped result but has no run
  orchestrator, so durable tool-call audit projection remains covered by the
  run-recorder suite.
- Exact counts intentionally make implementation-cost changes visible. A
  legitimate engine change may require a reviewed registry count update even
  when the semantic outcome is unchanged.
- The legacy successful-rung `errorCode: null` fixture remains intentionally
  checked in to prove old artifacts normalize; current tool output may not emit
  that shape.
